title: Pony.ai and Uber to put more than 2,000 Chinese robotaxis on European streets
excerpt: Pony.ai and Uber are expanding their partnership to deploy over 2,000 robotaxis across Europe, starting in Zagreb, in an asset-light bet that puts Chinese self-driving tech on European kerbs.
content_html:
Pony.ai and Uber have expanded their partnership to put more than 2,000 robotaxis on European roads, a deal that hands one of China’s autonomous-driving champions a route onto the continent’s streets through an American app and a scattering of local fleet owners.

The arrangement is divided as Pony.ai supplies the Level 4 self-driving technology and the operational know-how, Uber provides the platform, meaning booking, payments and customer service, along with its considerable market reach, and local partners own and run the actual fleets. In Zagreb, that partner is Croatia’s Verne.

Zagreb goes first, launching on the Uber platform in 2026, with four more European cities to follow in phases and a Middle East deployment also pencilled in.

It is a familiar shape for Uber, which has spent the past year signing up self-driving suppliers rather than building its own, from Wayve robotaxis in London to a growing roster of partners elsewhere.

The logic is asset-light and, for a Chinese firm eyeing Europe, quietly clever. By letting local partners shoulder the cost of the vehicles and much of the regulatory paperwork, Pony.ai sidesteps a good deal of the capital and compliance burden that has made robotaxi expansion so brutally expensive everywhere else.

It also plays to what Pony.ai already has. The company runs paid, fully driverless robotaxis in four Chinese cities and says it has reached city-wide breakeven unit economics in several markets, a claim few Western rivals can make with a straight face.

That track record is precisely what makes it useful to Uber, which would rather partner with a supplier that has already sweated the hard, expensive years of testing than start from scratch.

“By combining Pony.ai’s proven autonomous driving technology and operational know-how with Uber’s global mobility platform and extensive market reach, we aim to build sustained commercial operations at scale across Europe and beyond,” said Pony.ai chief executive Dr James Peng.

Uber and Pony.ai first joined forces in May 2025, and this fresh commitment scales that early pact up considerably. Sarfraz Maredia, who heads Uber’s autonomous mobility unit, framed Europe as the next proving ground for the tie-up.

There is a wrinkle, though, and it is a sizeable one. A Chinese self-driving system, hoovering up detailed mapping and movement data as it ferries passengers around European cities, arrives at a moment when Brussels is increasingly twitchy about Chinese technology, from electric vehicles to telecoms kit.

The data questions rather write themselves. Level 4 robotaxis are essentially rolling sensor arrays, and where all that footage and location data ends up being processed, stored and potentially accessed is precisely the sort of thing European regulators have already started asking of Chinese carmakers.

Uber, for its part, has been unusually candid about losing the self-driving race it once led. Having sold off its own autonomous unit years ago, it now positions itself as the neutral platform on which everyone else’s robots compete, and increasingly as the lobbyist writing the rulebook.

That pragmatism runs through its wider European ambitions. Uber is already testing Volkswagen’s MOIA minibuses and has run into trouble on the safety front too, with US regulators probing partner Avride after a spate of crashes in Dallas.

Whether European passengers will much care about the provenance of the car that pulls up is another matter entirely. For most riders, the deciding factors will be price, availability and, above all, whether the thing brakes in time.

What the deal makes plain is that the robotaxi race is no longer a purely American or Chinese affair played out on home turf.

Pony.ai’s arrival, via Uber’s app and a Croatian startup, is the moment the contest properly reaches the European kerb, and the moment Europe has to decide how comfortable it really is with whose software is doing the driving.

content_html_zh:
小马智行和 Uber 扩大了合作伙伴关系，在欧洲道路上投放了 2000 多辆机器人出租车，这项交易让中国自动驾驶冠军之一通过一款美国应用程序和分散的当地车队所有者获得了一条进入欧洲大陆街道的路线。

该安排分为小马智行提供 4 级自动驾驶技术和运营知识，优步提供平台，即预订、支付和客户服务及其相当大的市场覆盖范围，而当地合作伙伴拥有并运营实际车队。 在萨格勒布，这个合作伙伴是克罗地亚的凡尔纳。

萨格勒布率先推出，将于 2026 年在 Uber 平台上推出，随后将分阶段在另外四个欧洲城市跟进，并计划在中东进行部署。

对于 Uber 来说，这是一种熟悉的形式，从伦敦的 Wayve 机器人出租车到其他地方越来越多的合作伙伴，Uber 在过去的一年里一直在与自动驾驶供应商签约，而不是建立自己的供应商。

这个逻辑是轻资产的，对于一家着眼欧洲的中国公司来说，这是一个巧妙的逻辑。 通过让当地合作伙伴承担车辆成本和大部分监管文书工作，小马智行避开了大量资本和合规负担，而正是这些负担使得机器人出租车在其他地方的扩张成本极其昂贵。

它还发挥了 Pony.ai 已有的功能。 该公司在中国四个城市运营付费、完全无人驾驶的机器人出租车，并表示其在多个市场已实现全市范围内的单位经济效益盈亏平衡，很少有西方竞争对手能一本正经地宣称这一点。

这一记录正是它对 Uber 有用的地方，Uber 宁愿与已经经历了多年艰苦、昂贵的测试的供应商合作，也不愿从头开始。

“通过将小马智行成熟的自动驾驶技术和运营知识与优步的全球移动平台和广泛的市场覆盖相结合，我们的目标是在欧洲及其他地区建立大规模的持续商业运营，”小马智行首席执行官詹姆斯·彭博士表示。

Uber 和 Pony.ai 于 2025 年 5 月首次联手，这一新的承诺大大扩展了早期的协议。 Uber 自动驾驶移动部门负责人萨弗拉兹·马雷迪亚 (Sarfraz Maredia) 将欧洲视为此次合作的下一个试验场。

不过，有一个皱纹，而且是相当大的皱纹。 中国的自动驾驶系统在欧洲城市之间运送乘客时收集了详细的地图和移动数据，而在布鲁塞尔对从电动汽车到电信设备等中国技术越来越紧张的时刻到来。

数据问题而是自己写的。 4 级机器人出租车本质上是滚动传感器阵列，所有镜头和位置数据最终都会被处理、存储和潜在访问，这正是欧洲监管机构已经开始向中国汽车制造商提出的要求。

就优步而言，它对于输掉曾经领先的自动驾驶竞赛异常坦诚。 几年前，它出售了自己的自主部门，现在将自己定位为其他机器人竞争的中立平台，并且越来越多地成为编写规则手册的游说者。

这种实用主义贯穿了其更广泛的欧洲雄心。 Uber 已经在测试大众汽车的 MOIA 小型巴士，并且在安全方面也遇到了麻烦，美国监管机构在达拉斯发生一系列撞车事故后正在对合作伙伴 Avride 进行调查。

欧洲乘客是否会非常关心停下来的汽车的来源完全是另一回事。 对于大多数骑手来说，决定因素是价格、可用性，最重要的是刹车是否及时。

这笔交易清楚地表明，机器人出租车竞赛不再是纯粹在美国或中国本土进行的赛事。

Pony.ai 通过 Uber 的应用程序和克罗地亚初创公司的到来，是比赛正式进入欧洲赛道的时刻，也是欧洲必须决定由谁的软件来驾驶的时刻。
